newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: SPT says reverses Czech phone-wait trend.
newsitem.headline: SPT says reverses Czech phone-wait trend.

text.p: Czech telephone monopoly SPT Telecom said it had seen a surge in demand for new lines in 1996 but that the company had cut waiting lists to 623,000 by the end of the year from 650,000 at the end of 1995.
"That number (of those waiting) decreased for the first time in 10 years in 1996," said SPT deputy general director Bessel Kok.
The company said it intends to install 470,000 new lines in 1997 compared with just 400,000 for the whole of the 1980's.

In 1996, 417,000 new lines were installed and a further 100,000 global system for mobile (GSM) mobile handsets were sold by Eurotel, a majority-owned SPT subsidiary, bringing SPT's total number of new phone users to over 500,000.
"That's a huge effort by SPT Telecom...more than Holland and Switzerland put together," said Kok.
The fixed-line figures meant the number of lines per 100 inhabitants rose to 27.25 from 23.22 at the end of 1995.
SPT is managed by Swiss-Dutch consortium Telsource and it is under pressure to fulfill a government directive to almost double the number of lines installed by the year 2,000.
Kok, who is also the president of Telsource, said SPT had concentrated on those who had been on the waiting list the longest, especially those who had been waiting since before the end of 1990.

"There are still 30,000 customers in that catgory but...we have eliminated 88.2 percent of them (from the queue)," he said adding that there were people who had been waiting since the 1950's and that the oldest known and unfulfilled application had been made in 1927.
SPT Telecom plans to fully digitalise its network by the year 2,002 and has an 80 percent target for the year 2,000.
By the end of 1996, SPT said in a statement, the extent of digitalisation was approximaetly 33 percent versus 18 percent at the end of 1995.

A consortium of Royal PTT Netherlands and Swiss state operator Swiss Telecom won a 27 percent stake in SPT in 1995 for $1.32 billion in cash, and promised to expand the network to over four million lines by the end of the century.

They have also promised to make substantial upgrades in the quality of the system through a massive programme of digitalisation of switching stations and installation of fibre-optic and better copper cable.
